opus-5.5.text:
I think there are actually a lot of opportunities, and in some ways the compute constraint can push people toward the questions that matter most right now. One huge area is evaluation: figuring out what these systems can and can't actually do. We've seen over and over that a model can score impressively on a benchmark and then fall apart when you change the problem slightly, rephrase it, or move it a little away from what's likely in the training data. Designing careful experiments to probe whether a system really has a capability like abstraction, analogy, or causal reasoning doesn't require training a giant model. It requires good scientific thinking, and frankly the field needs a lot more of that.

Related to that is borrowing methods from cognitive science and developmental psychology. Those fields have spent decades figuring out how to test whether a child or an animal really understands a concept, with controls, counterfactual variations, and attention to confounds. Bringing that rigor to AI is something a single researcher with API access or a modest open model can do.

Then there's work on smaller-scale systems and domains where you can actually understand what's going on, like my own long interest in analogy-making in idealized microdomains, or the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus. Those let you ask deep questions about generalization and concept formation without needing a data center. Interpretability work on smaller open models is also very accessible and important.

And finally, I'd encourage people to think about the conceptual and theoretical side: what do we even mean by "understanding" or "intelligence," and how would we know if a machine had it? Those questions are wide open, and you don't need a thousand GPUs to make progress on them. You need curiosity, skepticism, and a willingness to look carefully.

r001.rationale: The response calls for more scientific thinking and careful evaluation, but does not state that deep learning research has outpaced scientific understanding of how it works.

r002.rationale: It identifies interpretability work on smaller open models and studying smaller-scale systems as accessible ways to understand how AI systems work without a data center.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I get a lot, and honestly I think it's one of the more hopeful questions in the field right now, because the answer is that there's an enormous amount of important work that doesn't require training a frontier model.

The first thing I'd say is that evaluation is wide open. We have these systems that score very well on benchmarks, and we still have surprisingly poor understanding of what they can actually do. Designing careful experiments that probe whether a model has really grasped a concept, or whether it's picked up on some statistical shortcut, is something you can do with API access and a laptop. A lot of my own work on abstraction and analogy, looking at things like ConceptARC, has been exactly that kind of work. You don't need a cluster to construct a clever set of test cases. You need to think hard about what a concept is and how you'd distinguish genuine understanding from pattern matching.

Related to that, there's a lot of value in going back and checking claims. Papers come out saying a model has "emergent" ability X, or that it can reason about Y. Very often, when someone looks closely, the result turns out to be more fragile than advertised, or it depends on the specific phrasing, or the test set leaked into the training data. That kind of careful, skeptical, almost adversarial science is undervalued relative to how useful it is. And it's cheap.

Second, I'd point people toward cognitive science and the history of AI. Many of the questions people are wrestling with now, about what it means to understand, what analogy is, how concepts form, were studied for decades before deep learning. There's a lot of insight there that people in machine learning simply haven't read. Someone who can bridge those literatures and bring a well-designed psychological experiment to bear on a language model is in a good position.

Third, smaller models and simpler domains are underrated. You can learn a tremendous amount about generalization, compositionality, and the limits of these systems by working with models you can train yourself, on tasks you fully control. In some ways it's better science, because you know exactly what the model saw during training, which you almost never know for a large commercial system.

And finally, I'd say don't underestimate the value of clear thinking and clear writing. Part of what the field needs right now is people who can define terms carefully, who notice when a word like "reasoning" or "understanding" is being used in three different ways in the same paper, and who can design experiments that actually settle a question instead of just adding to the noise. That requires no compute at all. It just requires being willing to be rigorous when a lot of the incentives push toward speed.

So I'm actually fairly optimistic. The big labs have the compute, but they don't have a monopoly on good questions.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers have a poor understanding of what models can do, but does not state that deep learning work has outpaced scientific understanding of how it works.

r002.rationale: It recommends low-cost evaluation of model capabilities and testing claims, but does not clearly identify investigating how deep learning systems work as the opportunity.

astra-6.text:
I think there are a lot of opportunities, particularly if you’re interested in understanding these systems rather than simply building bigger ones. You don’t necessarily need huge compute resources to ask a good question about what a model has learned, where it fails, or whether it can generalize beyond the examples it’s seen.

One area I’m particularly interested in is abstraction and analogy. You can study those in fairly small, controlled settings. Can a system learn a concept and recognize it in a different context? What changes to a problem cause it to fail? Sometimes a carefully designed experiment can tell you more than running another enormous benchmark.

And I think there’s a lot of room for ideas from cognitive science and psychology—both in designing tasks and in thinking about what counts as evidence of understanding. So my advice would be to find a specific question that really interests you, and figure out the simplest setting in which you can make progress on it. Having access to the most compute isn’t the same thing as having the most useful research question.

r001.rationale: The response discusses studying models, but does not say that deep learning work has outpaced scientific understanding of how it works.

r002.rationale: It identifies understanding models—such as what they learn, where they fail, and whether they generalize—as research that can be pursued without huge compute resources.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are a lot of opportunities, particularly if you’re interested in understanding intelligence rather than just building bigger systems. Having limited compute can push you to ask more focused questions: What does a system actually learn? When does it generalize, and when does it fail?

In my own area of interest, analogy and abstraction, you can study those questions with relatively small problems. Can a system learn a concept and recognize it in a different setting? Can it distinguish the underlying relationship from superficial similarities? You don’t necessarily need a huge model to do interesting work on that.

There’s also a lot to do in evaluation. Designing a good experiment that reveals something we didn’t understand about a system can be a substantial contribution. So I’d encourage someone starting out to find a question they really care about and think about the smallest experiment that could give them insight into it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses opportunities to study learning and generalization, but does not say that deep learning research has outpaced scientific understanding of how it works.

r002.rationale: It presents studying what a system learns as an opportunity that can use small problems, but does not clearly identify the systems as deep learning systems.
